The station with the largest absolute loss is Pioneer, which loses about 8,067 morning tap-ins per weekday (-70%). Before the new lines it is the most likely boarding station for a broad belt of Jurong West. Afterwards, the number of subzones in which it has at least a 20% share falls from 9 to 2. Its residential market shrinks from about 89,944 to 26,933 “expected residents” as Gek Poh, Tawas and Jurong West stations open inside its former catchment. It keeps a smaller walk-in core around the station itself.

10 Value-added analysis

Two additional analyses address questions the core Huff model cannot answer:

  1. Are the low-boarding JRL stations really “ghost stations”? The Huff model only sees home-end demand. An alternative probabilistic spatial interaction model, the Multiplicative Competitive Interaction (MCI) model, is calibrated on observed station-to-station choice shares to predict destination-end demand at the new stations (Section 10.1).
  2. Are the Huff model’s errors spatially structured? (Section 10.2)

10.1 An alternative probabilistic SIM: MCI destination-choice model

Question. 9 new stations fall below today’s lower quartile of morning boardings (Figure 9). Most sit in the Jurong industrial estate, the NTU campus or the Changi aviation cluster, places people travel to in the morning rather than from. A home-end model cannot tell whether these stations will be busy as destinations, so the “ghost-risk” label may be wrong for some of them.

Method. The MCI model (Nakanishi & Cooper, 1974), the second probabilistic model in the MCI package, describes how passengers boarding at station i choose where to alight:

\[p_{ij} = \frac{\prod_k X_{kj}^{\beta_k}\; d_{ij}^{\beta_d}}{\sum_{l \ne i} \prod_k X_{kl}^{\beta_k}\; d_{il}^{\beta_d}}\]

Here \(d_{ij}\) is the rail network distance and the \(X_{kj}\) are destination attributes: job, education and residential floor area within 800 m (from the Master Plan land use), lines served, and an MRT indicator. Unlike the Huff model, which assumes its parameters, the MCI model is estimated from observed choice shares, here the weekday morning-peak flows between all pairs of the 164 stations. The log-centering transformation turns it into a linear regression whose coefficients are the elasticities \(\beta\).

Two implementation choices need explaining:

  • A custom estimator. MCI::mci.transmat() and mci.fit() assume every origin faces the same set of destinations. In station-to-station data the boarding station itself is never a destination, so each origin has a different choice set of 163 stations. The log-centering transformation is therefore applied with dplyr and estimated by OLS. The first chunk confirms that this reproduces MCI::mci.fit() exactly on a complete matrix.
  • A continuity correction. About 15% of station pairs have zero observed flow, and log-centering cannot take logs of zero, so 0.5 trips are added to every pair. This is the standard correction for zero cells in log-linear models.
Show code 
lc_fit <- function(df, origin, vars, share) {
  lc <- df %>%
    group_by(.data[[origin]]) %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(c(share, vars)), \(x) log(x) - mean(log(x)), .names = "{.col}_lc")) %>%
    ungroup()
  lm(as.formula(str_c(share, "_lc ~ 0 + ", str_c(vars, "_lc", collapse = " + "))), data = lc)
}

# Check against MCI::mci.fit() on a complete synthetic interaction matrix
set.seed(626)
toy <- expand_grid(origin = sprintf("o%02d", 1:15), store = sprintf("s%02d", 1:8)) %>%
  mutate(dist = runif(n(), 0.5, 10), size = runif(n(), 1, 50),
         u = size^0.8 * dist^-1.5 * exp(rnorm(n(), 0, 0.2))) %>%
  group_by(origin) %>% mutate(share = u / sum(u)) %>% ungroup() %>% as.data.frame()

rbind(MCI_package = coef(mci.fit(toy, "origin", "store", "share", "dist", "size")),
      custom      = coef(lc_fit(toy, "origin", c("dist", "size"), "share")))
               dist_t    size_t
MCI_package -1.509222 0.7657308
custom      -1.509222 0.7657308

The two estimators agree to every decimal place.

Show code 
mci_vars <- c("net_km", "d_job", "d_edu", "d_res", "d_lines", "d_mrt")

make_mci <- function(dist_mat, stn_tbl) {
  expand_grid(orig = stn_tbl$stn_code, dest = stn_tbl$stn_code) %>%
    filter(orig != dest) %>%
    mutate(net_km = pmax(dist_mat[cbind(orig, dest)], 0.5)) %>%
    left_join(stn_tbl %>% transmute(dest = stn_code,
                                    d_job = job_ha + 1, d_edu = edu_ha + 1, d_res = res_ha + 1,
                                    d_lines = n_lines,
                                    d_mrt = if_else(lrt, 1, exp(1))),   # dummy coded as e^D
              by = "dest")
}

base_tbl <- destination_df %>% filter(status == "Existing")
mci_base <- make_mci(net_dist, base_tbl) %>%
  left_join(sim_data %>% select(orig, dest, trips), by = c("orig", "dest")) %>%
  mutate(trips = replace_na(trips, 0)) %>%
  group_by(orig) %>% mutate(p_ij = (trips + 0.5) / sum(trips + 0.5)) %>% ungroup()

mci_fit  <- lc_fit(mci_base, "orig", mci_vars, "p_ij")
mci_null <- lc_fit(mci_base, "orig", "net_km", "p_ij")
b_mci <- setNames(coef(mci_fit), mci_vars)

mci_predict <- function(df, O) {
  df %>%
    mutate(u = exp(as.numeric(as.matrix(log(df[mci_vars])) %*% b_mci))) %>%
    group_by(orig) %>% mutate(p = u / sum(u)) %>% ungroup() %>%
    left_join(O, by = "orig") %>%
    mutate(flow = p * O)
}

O_obs <- sim_data %>% group_by(orig) %>% summarise(O = sum(trips))

  summarise(observed = sum(trips), predicted = sum(flow))

tibble(pair_R2 = cor(mci_in$trips, mci_in$flow)^2,
       alighting_R2 = cor(alight_fit$observed, alight_fit$predicted)^2)

Robustness: OpenStreetMap POIs as alternative attractors. The handout recommends OSM points of interest, so the model is re-estimated with POI counts within 800 m (food & retail, education, health, leisure & civic), first added to and then replacing the land-use attractors.

Show code 
mci_base_poi <- mci_base %>%
  left_join(base_tbl %>% transmute(dest = stn_code, d_food = poi_food_retail + 1,
                                   d_poi_edu = poi_edu + 1, d_health = poi_health + 1,
                                   d_leisure = poi_leisure_civic + 1), by = "dest")
poi_vars <- c("d_food", "d_poi_edu", "d_health", "d_leisure")

                 "Land use + OSM POIs" = c(mci_vars, poi_vars),
                 "OSM POIs instead of land use" = c("net_km", poi_vars, "d_lines", "d_mrt"))

imap_dfr(spec_mci, \(vv, nm) {
  f <- lc_fit(mci_base_poi, "orig", vv, "p_ij")
  b <- setNames(coef(f), vv)
  pr <- mci_base_poi %>%
    mutate(u = exp(as.numeric(as.matrix(log(mci_base_poi[vv])) %*% b))) %>%
    group_by(orig) %>% mutate(p = u / sum(u)) %>% ungroup() %>%
    left_join(O_obs, by = "orig") %>% mutate(flow = p * O)
  al <- pr %>% group_by(dest) %>% summarise(obs = sum(trips), pred = sum(flow))
  tibble(specification = nm, parameters = length(vv),
         adj_R2_log_centered = summary(f)$adj.r.squared,
         alighting_R2 = cor(al$obs, al$pred)^2)
}) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

The POIs add almost nothing, and the reason matters for forecasting. Adding them to the land-use model barely changes the log-centered fit, and the POI coefficients take conflicting signs because POI counts are strongly correlated with each other and with land use. Replacing land use with POIs gives a similar fit for existing stations. For new stations, however, the two sources diverge sharply: Jurong Pier, Tukang, Loyang and Aviation Park have almost no POIs today but hundreds of hectares of planned job floor space. OpenStreetMap records what has been built, while the Master Plan records what is planned. For predicting stations that open in 2028–2030 in areas still under development, the Master Plan land use is the appropriate attractor, so it is retained.

Estimated model. The coefficients behave as a destination model should:

  • Distance: a 1% longer network trip lowers a destination’s share by about 1.29%.
  • Rail service: an MRT station draws about \(e^{\beta} \approx\) 11 times the share of an otherwise similar LRT-only halt, and each doubling of lines served multiplies the share by about 1.9.
  • Jobs and education: job floor space (t = 11) and education floor space (t = 4) both raise a destination’s share.
  • Residential floor space: no effect (t = -0.3). This is expected, since morning trips end at workplaces and schools, not at homes, and it confirms that the model separates destination demand from the home-end demand handled by the Huff model.
  • Fit: the attributes raise the adjusted R² of the log-centered model from 0.18 (distance only) to 0.43, and the model reproduces total morning alightings at existing stations with R² = 0.34.

Most of the remaining variation comes from destinations the attributes cannot describe, such as hospitals, the airport and major schools. The fit is therefore weaker than that of a doubly constrained SIM (explored in Section 15). The trade-off is deliberate: the doubly constrained SIM cannot be applied to a station that does not yet exist, whereas the MCI model can.

Prediction for the 2030 network. The calibrated MCI model is applied to the expanded network (193 stations, network distances recomputed on the expanded rail graph). Morning boardings at every station come from the Huff scenario, so the two models are chained: Huff → where residents board, MCI → where those passengers alight.

       y = "Predicted AM-peak alightings per weekday (MCI, log)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
Show code 
new_use_sf <- new_stations %>%
  left_join(new_use %>% select(stn_code, board_day, alight_day, total_day, role), by = "stn_code") %>%
  st_transform(4326)
pal_role <- colorFactor(c("#d95f02", "#176b87", "#7570b3"),
                        levels = c("Destination station", "Home station", "Mixed"))
max_use <- max(new_use_sf$total_day)

base_leaflet() %>%
  add_network(new_links = TRUE) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(data = new_use_sf %>% arrange(desc(total_day)), group = "New stations",
                   radius = ~radius_of(total_day, max_use, 22), color = "white", weight = 1,
                   fillColor = ~pal_role(role), fillOpacity = 0.85,
                   label = ~str_to_title(stn_name),
                   popup = ~sprintf("<b>%s</b> (%s)<br>Boardings: %s / weekday<br>Alightings: %s / weekday<br>Total: %s / weekday<br>%s",
                                    str_to_title(stn_name), line, comma(round(board_day)),
                                    comma(round(alight_day)), comma(round(total_day)), role)) %>%
  addLegend("bottomright", pal = pal_role, values = new_use_sf$role, opacity = 0.9,
            title = "Station role") %>%
  add_size_legend(c(1000, 5000, 15000), max_use, "Total AM use per weekday", max_r = 22) %>%
  layer_control(c("New stations", "Rail network"))

Insight. Adding destination demand changes the ghost-station verdict.

  • 13 of the 29 new stations are destination stations, where predicted alightings exceed boardings by more than half: Tengah, Enterprise, Tukang, Jurong Hill, Jurong Pier, Nanyang Gateway, Nanyang Crescent, Peng Kang Hill, Jurong Town Hall, Aviation Park, Loyang, Defu, Tavistock. They serve the Jurong industrial estate and Jurong Innovation District, the Loyang, Defu and aviation employment areas, the NTU campus and the Tengah town centre.
  • 4 stations are “rescued” from ghost risk: Tengah, Loyang, Tukang, Nanyang Gateway. They fall below the lower quartile on boardings, but their combined morning use clears the lower quartile of existing stations. Judging them on boardings alone, as the Huff model must, would wrongly label them white elephants.
  • 5 stations remain below the lower quartile even with destination demand: Aviation Park, Peng Kang Hill, Nanyang Crescent, Jurong Pier, Jurong Hill. These are the genuine opening-day risks, and each has an explanation the planner should weigh:
    • Jurong Hill and Jurong Pier depend on industrial land that is still being redeveloped.
    • Nanyang Crescent and Peng Kang Hill serve the NTU campus, where students in campus halls are under-counted in the Census subzone population and the university is coded as one large educational parcel.
    • Aviation Park serves an airport-logistics cluster with shift-based demand outside the morning peak.

Assumptions and limitations.

  • The MCI model inherits the independence of irrelevant alternatives: a new destination draws passengers from all other destinations in proportion to their current shares.
  • Land-use floor area is a proxy for jobs, not an employment count.
  • The 0.5-trip continuity correction slightly inflates the shares of very unattractive pairs.
  • The chained Huff → MCI prediction carries the fixed-population assumption of the Huff scenario.

Even so, the MCI model adds substantive insight that the core analysis lacked. It separates stations that will be empty from stations that will be busy at the other end of the trip, and that distinction should drive any decision to defer or reprioritise station openings.

10.2 Spatial autocorrelation of Huff residuals

Question. The Huff model assumes that, once distance and attraction are accounted for, the remaining errors are independent. If residuals cluster spatially, some spatial process is missing, for example town-level feeder-bus networks, and predictions in that area will be biased in a consistent direction.

Method. A k-nearest-neighbour weights matrix (k = 6, about the number of adjacent stations in Singapore’s network) is built over station locations. Global Moran’s I is tested by a 999-permutation Monte Carlo test, and local Moran’s I (LISA) identifies where clusters occur (Chapters 9–10). The k-nearest-neighbour scheme is used because stations are points with very unequal spacing: a distance band would leave Tuas stations with no neighbours and give CBD stations dozens.

Show code 
nb_knn <- knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(res_map), k = 6))
lw_knn <- nb2listw(nb_knn, style = "W")

moran_mc <- moran.mc(res_map$residual, lw_knn, nsim = 999)
moran_mc

    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  res_map$residual 
weights: lw_knn  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.19423, observed rank = 1000, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater
Show code 
# Robustness of the global test to the neighbour definition
map_dfr(c(4, 6, 8, 10), \(k) {
  lw <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(res_map), k = k)), style = "W")
  m <- moran.mc(res_map$residual, lw, nsim = 999)
  tibble(k = k, moran_I = round(m$statistic, 3), pseudo_p = m$p.value)
})
k moran_I pseudo_p
4 0.206 0.001
6 0.194 0.001
8 0.203 0.001
10 0.205 0.001
Show code 
lisa <- localmoran(res_map$residual, lw_knn)
z_res <- as.numeric(scale(res_map$residual))
lag_res <- lag.listw(lw_knn, z_res)
res_map <- res_map %>%
  mutate(p_lisa = lisa[, 5],
         cluster = case_when(
           p_lisa >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant",
           z_res > 0 & lag_res > 0 ~ "High-High (under-predicted cluster)",
           z_res < 0 & lag_res < 0 ~ "Low-Low (over-predicted cluster)",
           z_res > 0 & lag_res < 0 ~ "High-Low",
           TRUE ~ "Low-High"))
count(st_drop_geometry(res_map), cluster)

Show code 
lisa_levels <- c("High-High (under-predicted cluster)", "Low-Low (over-predicted cluster)",
                 "High-Low", "Low-High", "Not significant")
lisa_view <- res_map %>% mutate(cluster = factor(cluster, levels = lisa_levels)) %>% st_transform(4326)
pal_lisa <- colorFactor(c("#2166ac", "#b2182b", "#92c5de", "#f4a582", "#bdbdbd"), levels = lisa_levels)
max_res <- max(abs(lisa_view$residual)) / weekdays_may22

base_leaflet() %>%
  add_network() %>%
  addCircleMarkers(data = lisa_view, group = "Stations",
                   radius = ~radius_of(abs(residual) / weekdays_may22, max_res), color = "#555", weight = 0.6,
                   fillColor = ~pal_lisa(cluster), fillOpacity = 0.85,
                   label = ~str_to_title(stn_name),
                   popup = ~sprintf("<b>%s</b><br>Residual: %s tap-ins / weekday<br>%s",
                                    str_to_title(stn_name), comma(round(residual / weekdays_may22)), cluster)) %>%
  addLegend("bottomright", pal = pal_lisa, values = lisa_view$cluster, opacity = 0.9,
            title = "LISA cluster") %>%
  add_size_legend(c(1000, 3000, 7000), max_res, "|Residual| per weekday") %>%
  layer_control(c("Stations", "Rail network"))

Insight. Global Moran’s I is 0.194 (pseudo p = 0.001). It stays positive and significant for every neighbour definition from k = 4 to k = 10, so the Huff residuals are regionally clustered, not independent. The LISA map locates two main regimes:

  • Under-predicted (High-High) clusters: the northern NSL corridor (Kranji, Marsiling, Woodlands, Yishun), consistent with cross-border commuters and long-distance feeder buses, and the Orchard–Novena–Stevens city-fringe belt (Novena, Orchard, Somerset, Stevens), where schools, hotels and medical facilities generate non-residential morning boardings.
  • Over-predicted (Low-Low) cluster: the east (Bedok, Bedok North, Bedok Reservoir, Expo, Pasir Ris, Tampines East, Tampines, Tampines West, Tanah Merah, Upper Changi), where dense direct bus services to the Tampines regional centre and the Changi employment areas compete with rail.

What this adds. The core model’s fit statistics say how much error there is; the spatial test shows the error is regional, which matters for forecasting. The CRL1 stations in the east (Pasir Ris East, Tampines North, Loyang and Aviation Park) sit inside the over-predicted cluster, so their forecasts in Figure 9 should be read as upper bounds. The JRL stations sit in the west, where no significant residual cluster is detected, so there is no evidence of a regional bias in their forecasts. A future model could absorb the eastern effect with a regional dummy or a bus-competition variable.

Assumptions and limitations. The k = 6 neighbour definition was chosen a priori; the robustness table shows the conclusion holds for k = 4 to 10. Moran’s I on residuals tests for clustering but cannot identify its cause. With 164 points, local tests also carry a multiple-testing risk, so isolated significant stations should not be over-interpreted.

11 Station-by-station verdict

The analyses above each look at the new stations from one angle. Table 1 brings them together into one verdict per station. The categories are assigned in order, and each rests on a result from this report:

  1. Opening-day risk: below the lower quartile of existing stations even after adding MCI destination demand (Section 10.1).
  2. Depends on future housing: boardings at least double when Tengah is built out (Section 7.3).
  3. Destination-led: predicted morning alightings exceed boardings by more than half; the station is busy as a place people travel to (Section 10.1).
  4. Strong from day one: predicted boardings in the top quarter of existing stations under both Model 4 and Model 6 (Section 6.6).
  5. Moderate: the remaining stations, in the normal range of today’s network.
Show code 
p75_day <- quantile(y_obs, 0.75) / weekdays_may22
buildout <- tibble(stn_code = scenario$stn_code, buildout_day = pred_tengah / weekdays_may22)

verdict <- new_use %>%
  left_join(m46 %>% select(stn_code, m6), by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(buildout, by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(destination_df %>% select(stn_code, hdb_ha_800m), by = "stn_code") %>%
  mutate(verdict = case_when(
    ghost_by_total_use ~ "Opening-day risk",
    buildout_day >= 2 * board_day ~ "Depends on future housing",
    role == "Destination station" ~ "Destination-led",
    board_day > p75_day & m6 > p75_day ~ "Strong from day one",
    TRUE ~ "Moderate"),
    verdict = factor(verdict, levels = c("Strong from day one", "Moderate", "Destination-led",
                                         "Depends on future housing", "Opening-day risk")))

verdict %>%
  arrange(verdict, desc(board_day)) %>%
  transmute(Station = str_to_title(stn_name), Line = line, Verdict = verdict,
            `Boardings (M4)` = fmt(board_day), `Boardings (M6)` = fmt(m6),
            Alightings = fmt(alight_day), `At build-out` = fmt(buildout_day),
            `HDB 800 m (ha)` = round(hdb_ha_800m))

Read together, the verdicts sort the new stations into five clear groups:

  • Strong from day one (3): Choa Chu Kang West, Pasir Ris East, Serangoon North. They open into mature HDB estates and would rank in the top quarter of today’s stations under both models.
  • Moderate (11): Corporation, Jurong West, Bahar Junction, Gek Poh, Tawas, Tengah Park, Bukit Batok West, Toh Guan, Pandan Reservoir, Tampines North, Teck Ghee. In the normal range of today’s network; no special action is needed beyond normal feeder-bus planning.
  • Destination-led (7): Enterprise, Tukang, Nanyang Gateway, Jurong Town Hall, Loyang, Defu, Tavistock. Low on home-based boardings but busy as morning destinations; they should be appraised on total use.
  • Depends on future housing (3): Tengah, Hong Kah, Tengah Plantation. Their case rests on Tengah filling up, so opening dates and service levels should follow housing completions.
  • Opening-day risk (5): Jurong Hill, Jurong Pier, Nanyang Crescent, Peng Kang Hill, Aviation Park. Low under every measure in this report; each needs an explicit case based on workers, students or shift-based demand that a morning residential model cannot see.

12 Discussion and planning implications

Addressing the objectives.

  • O1. A Huff model with three station attributes (lines served, LRT status and HDB housing within 800 m) and an exponential access-distance decay (\(\hat\lambda \approx\) 1.83 per km) explains about 81% of the variation in morning boardings across 164 stations. It holds up out of sample (cross-validated R² 0.79) and clearly beats the nearest-station (0.44) and default-Huff (0.48) benchmarks. The MCI destination-choice model (Section 10.1) adds the other end of the trip.
  • O2. The strongest new stations are those inserted into mature HDB estates that currently lack a walkable MRT station, led by Pasir Ris East, Serangoon North and Choa Chu Kang West. CRL1 stations average almost twice the JRL’s morning boardings. 9 stations, all in employment areas, at NTU or in Tengah, fall below today’s lower quartile on boardings. The MCI destination model shows that 4 of them (Tengah, Loyang, Tukang, Nanyang Gateway) are busy enough as morning destinations to clear that bar, leaving 5 genuine opening-day risks.
  • O3. Under fixed population the new lines redistribute, rather than create, morning boardings (about 12% moves to the new stations). Losses are concentrated in three clusters beside the new lines. Pioneer, Lakeside and Chinese Garden lose more than half their boardings, and four of the seven upgraded interchanges still lose tap-ins to new stations inside their catchments.

Implications for sustainable rail planning.

  1. Judge a new station by the housing around it, not by the network average. Morning boardings follow the housing within walking distance (Section 7.2). 10 new stations have almost no HDB housing within 800 m and are forecast to be among the quietest in the network; their case must rest on workers, students or future housing, and should be made explicitly.
  2. Phase JRL openings to housing completions. The Tengah sensitivity shows that the decisive variable is residents, not rails. A completion-linked threshold, using this model to estimate boardings at each stage of build-out, gives operators a transparent basis for deciding whether to open, partially open or defer a station, which is the decision faced at Hume and Buangkok.
  3. Re-plan feeder buses around the losing stations. The stations losing 15% or more of morning boardings (the Jurong West EWL stations, the Bukit Panjang LRT, and the Kovan–Serangoon–Bishan belt) are where feeder routes should be re-drawn, so that bus kilometres follow the new market areas instead of duplicating rail.
  4. Plan interchange capacity, not just new stations. Even where an upgraded interchange loses tap-ins, it gains transfers, which tap-in data do not record. Platform and corridor capacity at the seven interchanges is where crowding risk rises first.
  5. Appraise stations on both ends of the trip. The chained Huff → MCI forecast shows that 13 of the 29 new stations are destination stations. Station-level appraisals should combine home-end and destination-end demand; either alone would mis-rank the stations.
  6. Read eastern forecasts as upper bounds. The residual clustering shows the model systematically over-predicts in the east, so Pasir Ris East, Tampines North and Loyang may under-perform their forecasts.

13 Limitations

  • Temporal mismatch. OD flows are from May 2022 and population is from Census 2020; the scenario network is planned for 2028–2030. Population growth outside Tengah (for example, Tampines North and Bayshore) is not modelled.
  • Fixed total demand. The trip rate \(k\) is fixed, so the model cannot represent induced demand from better connectivity, and new-station boardings are entirely diverted from existing stations. True totals will be higher.
  • Attraction variables. \(A_j\) contains line count, LRT status and HDB footprint within 800 m. HDB footprint is a proxy for homes and ignores private housing and occupancy; feeder-bus strength, cross-border demand, competing bus services, station amenities and service frequency are missing, as the significant residual clustering confirms. New stations are assumed to behave like an average single-line MRT station.
  • Distance. Straight-line distance from subzone population-weighted centroids is used for station access. Walking-network or travel-time distances, for example from sfnetworks on an OSM path network, would be more realistic, especially across expressways and canals.
  • Morning peak only. The Huff model explains home-end boardings and the MCI model explains morning destinations. Neither covers off-peak, evening or shift-work demand, which matters for stations such as Aviation Park.
  • Station coordinates. New-station locations come from indicative Master Plan footprints and the station list from LTA announcements. Working names and exact locations may still change.

14 Conclusion

A carefully cleaned dataset and a parsimonious, well-validated Huff model give planners a transparent way to forecast boardings at stations that do not yet exist. For the JRL and CRL1, the model gives a clear and actionable picture. Stations dropped into mature estates open into ready-made demand, while stations with little housing within walking distance, in industrial estates, at NTU, near the airport or in the still-filling new town of Tengah, are forecast to have very low ridership. Much of the JRL is a bet on future housing, and that bet can be managed by tying station openings to housing completions. The impacts on existing stations are local, predictable and largest along the western EWL.

15 Further exploration: station-to-station spatial interaction models

The Huff and MCI models above are the appropriate tools for the research question, because they model a resident’s choice among competing stations and can be applied to stations that do not exist yet. This section records an additional exploration: the generic Chapter 16 family of spatial interaction models (SIMs), fitted to station-to-station flows. These models describe how far people ride once on the network rather than which station they board at, and the doubly constrained version cannot be applied to a new station. They are therefore kept as background, not as part of the forecast.

15.1 Distance measure

The flow data frame sim_data (Section 5) holds every station pair, including zero-flow pairs, with two distance measures: straight-line distance, and network distance along the rail graph, which is closer to what passengers actually travel. Two stations on either side of a river may be close in a straight line but far apart by rail.

Show code 
dbc_euc <- glm(trips ~ orig + dest + log(euc_km), family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data)
dbc_net <- glm(trips ~ orig + dest + log(net_km), family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data)

CalcRSquared <- function(observed, estimated) cor(observed, estimated)^2

tibble(distance = c("Euclidean", "Network"),
       beta_distance = c(coef(dbc_euc)["log(euc_km)"], coef(dbc_net)["log(net_km)"]),
       AIC = c(AIC(dbc_euc), AIC(dbc_net)),
       R2 = c(CalcRSquared(sim_data$trips, fitted(dbc_euc)),
              CalcRSquared(sim_data$trips, fitted(dbc_net))))
distance beta_distance AIC R2
Euclidean -0.8649965 9251197 0.5843233
Network -0.9325878 7839822 0.5953035

Network distance gives the lower AIC and the higher R², so it is used for the SIM family below.

15.2 Calibrating the four SIMs

The origin attribute is residential intensity (HDB footprint within 800 m, a proxy for the people who can walk to the station). The destination attributes are service level (d_lines) and LRT status. These are the station-level analogues of the age-band population variables used in Chapter 16.

Show code 
sim_models <- list(
  unconstrained = glm(trips ~ log(o_hdb) + log(d_lines) + d_lrt + log(net_km),
                      family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data),
  origin_constrained = glm(trips ~ orig + log(d_lines) + d_lrt + log(net_km),
                           family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data),
  destination_constrained = glm(trips ~ dest + log(o_hdb) + log(net_km),
                                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data),
  doubly_constrained = glm(trips ~ orig + dest + log(net_km),
                           family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data))

sim_summary <- imap_dfr(sim_models, \(m, nm) tibble(
  model = nm,
  beta_distance = coef(m)["log(net_km)"],
  beta_origin_hdb = coef(m)["log(o_hdb)"],
  beta_dest_lines = coef(m)["log(d_lines)"],
  beta_dest_lrt = coef(m)["d_lrt"],
  R2 = CalcRSquared(sim_data$trips, fitted(m)),
  RMSE = sqrt(mean((sim_data$trips - fitted(m))^2))))

sim_summary %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

Show code 
sim_fit <- imap(sim_models, \(m, nm) {
  tibble(obs = sim_data$trips, fit = fitted(m)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(fit + 1, obs + 1)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.08, size = 0.5, colour = "#176b87") +
    geom_abline(linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
    scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) + scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
    labs(title = str_replace(nm, "_", " "),
         subtitle = str_c("R² = ", round(CalcRSquared(sim_data$trips, fitted(m)), 3)),
         x = "Fitted trips + 1", y = "Observed trips + 1") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
})
ggarrange(plotlist = sim_fit, ncol = 2, nrow = 2)

15.3 Interpretation

  • Constraints matter most. Fit rises from R² = 0.12 (unconstrained) to 0.6 (doubly constrained). Station-specific origin and destination effects therefore explain far more of the flow pattern than the few attributes we can measure. Unmeasured destination pull from employment, schools and malls is the main omitted factor, which the destination fixed effects absorb.
  • Distance decay is modest. In the doubly constrained model, a 1% increase in network distance reduces expected flow by about 0.93%. Rail is used for long, cross-island trips; this elasticity is far weaker than the access-distance decay of the Huff model (Section 6), because people choose a station within walking or feeder range but will ride that station’s line across the island.
  • LRT destinations attract fewer trips (negative d_lrt), and more lines attract more trips (positive d_lines). Both signs agree with the Huff calibration in Section 6, which is reassuring.
  • Limitations. The doubly constrained model cannot predict flows for a station with no history, because it needs a fixed effect for every origin and destination. This is why it remains an explanatory exploration, and the Huff and MCI models carry the predictive step. The Poisson models also assume equidispersion. With 15% zero pairs and heavy-tailed counts the flows are overdispersed, so standard errors are too small and coefficients should be read as effect sizes, not tested for significance.

# Introduction

## Setting the scene

Singapore builds MRT stations years before the surrounding towns fill up. Hume station sat as a finished shell for a decade, and Buangkok and Woodleigh stayed shut when the North-East Line opened in 2003 because SBS Transit judged their expected ridership too low to cover operating costs. Two new lines are now under construction. The **Jurong Region Line (JRL)** has 24 stations opening in three stages from mid-2028 to 2029. **Cross Island Line Phase 1 (CRL1)** has 12 stations from Aviation Park to Bright Hill and is due in 2030. Planners therefore need a defensible way to estimate how many people each new station will attract and which existing stations will lose riders to them.

## Research question and objectives

> **Research question:** Can a probabilistic spatial interaction model calibrated on observed tap-in data reproduce station-level ridership on Singapore's current rail network well enough to estimate demand at the 29 new JRL/CRL1 stations, and to show how those stations reshape the market areas of existing stations?

| # | Objective (handout) | Where it is addressed |
|---|---|---|
| O1 | Calibrate a probabilistic spatial interaction model for station-level ridership | @sec-huff (Huff model) and @sec-va-mci (MCI model) |
| O2 | Predict ridership of the proposed JRL and CRL1 stations | @sec-scenario |
| O3 | Evaluate the impact of the new stations on existing stations | @sec-impact and @sec-market |

The eight handout tasks map onto the report as follows: the two spatial interaction data frames, the origin data frame and the destination data frame (Tasks 1–3) are built in @sec-sidf; calibration and estimation (Tasks 4–6) are in @sec-huff, with an MCI destination-choice model in @sec-va-mci; prediction and impact (Tasks 7–8) are in @sec-scenario to @sec-market.

## Analytical framework

The study uses the two probabilistic models of the `MCI` package.

1. **Huff model (Chapter 18).** Each resident subzone is treated as a market and each station as a competing "store". The probability that residents of subzone *i* board at station *j* is

$$P_{ij} = \frac{A_j \, f(d_{ij})}{\sum_{k} A_k \, f(d_{ik})}, \qquad A_j = n^{\gamma}_{j}\,e^{\delta \cdot LRT_j}\,\left(\frac{HDB_j}{10}\right)^{\theta}$$

where $f(d_{ij})$ is a distance-decay function (power or exponential; @sec-huff selects between them), $n_j$ is the number of rail lines serving the station, $LRT_j$ flags LRT-only stations and $HDB_j$ is the HDB footprint (ha) within 800 m of the station. Expected boardings at station *j* are $\hat{B}_j = k\sum_i P_{ij}\,Pop_i$, where $k$ is a system trip rate. Parameters $\gamma$, $\delta$, $\theta$ and $\lambda$ are calibrated against observed **weekday morning-peak tap-ins**, and the fitted model is then re-run with the new stations added.
2. **MCI destination-choice model** (@sec-va-mci). Estimated from observed station-to-station flows, it predicts where morning passengers *alight*, the destination end that a residential Huff model cannot see.

The Huff model is the main prediction engine because it can price in a station that has no ridership history yet: all it needs is the station's location and attributes. Generic station-to-station spatial interaction models (Chapter 16) were also explored; they cannot forecast a new station, so they are reported at the end as further exploration (@sec-sim).

## Key assumptions and methodological decisions

| Decision | Choice made | Reason | Alternative tested or rejected |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dependent variable | Weekday 06:00–09:59 tap-ins | Home-based boardings match a residential demand model | Total daily ridership, which mixes in destination demand |
| Origins | 286 populated subzones with HDB-weighted centroids | Places demand where residents actually live | Plain polygon centroids |
| Station coordinates | SVY21 `X`/`Y`, falling back to lat/long | Lat/long misplaces Rochor by about 350 m; confirmed against LTA station exits (@sec-quality) | Lat/long throughout |
| Destination attractors (MCI) | Master Plan job/education floor area | Captures *planned* development around new stations | OSM POIs, which record only what exists today |
| Future stations | 29 new + 7 upgraded interchanges (official JRL/CRL1 list) | The URA layer mixes in 60+ non-JRL/CRL1 names | Naive name anti-join (98 "new" stations) |
| Attraction $A_j$ | Lines served, LRT penalty and HDB footprint within 800 m | Captures why stations in mature estates are busy and stations in new or non-residential districts are not | Lines + LRT only; closeness centrality; bus stops within 400 m (with and without HDB) |
| Distance decay | Exponential, calibrated $\lambda$ | Better fit; no unrealistic long tail | Power function (Chapter 18 default) |
| Calibration | RMSE minimised by `optim()`, 5-fold cross-validation | Unbounded search; out-of-sample check | Coarse fixed grid |
| Total demand | Fixed trip rate $k$ | Isolates the spatial reallocation effect | Tengah build-out sensitivity adds residents |
| Benchmarks | Nearest station; default Huff | The calibrated model must beat simple rules | – |

# Packages

The packages are loaded with `pacman::p_load()`, which installs any that are missing so the report renders end to end on a fresh machine.

| Package | Role in this study |
|---|---|
| `sf` | Import, project, join and measure geospatial data |
| `tidyverse` | Data wrangling (`dplyr`, `tidyr`, `stringr`) and graphics (`ggplot2`) |
| `igraph` | Build the rail network graph; network distances and centrality |
| `MCI` | Huff market shares (`huff.shares()`) and station totals (`shares.total()`) |
| `performance` | Model comparison for the Poisson SIMs (`compare_performance()`) |
| `spdep` | Spatial weights, global and local Moran's I on model residuals |
| `tmap` | Cartographic-quality thematic maps |
| `ggpubr`, `ggstatsplot` | Multi-panel diagnostics and observed-vs-predicted plots |
| `knitr` | Report tables |

```{r}
#| label: setup
pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, igraph, MCI, spdep, leaflet,
               tmap, performance, ggpubr, ggstatsplot, ggrepel, knitr, scales)

sf_use_s2(FALSE)           # planar geometry: all analysis is in SVY21 (EPSG:3414)
tmap_mode("plot")
set.seed(626)

fmt <- function(x, d = 0) scales::comma(x, accuracy = 10^-d)

# Interactive maps are drawn with leaflet on real basemaps. Esri tiles (as used in the
# course notes) need no API key; CARTO tiles now do. leaflet is used directly instead of
# tmap's view mode, whose legends draw oversized symbols and cannot show bubble sizes.
base_leaflet <- function(view = c(103.82, 1.355, 11)) {
  leaflet() %>%
    addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", group = "Grey canvas") %>%
    addProviderTiles("OpenStreetMap", group = "OpenStreetMap") %>%
    addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery", group = "Satellite") %>%
    setView(lng = view[1], lat = view[2], zoom = view[3])
}
layer_control <- function(m, overlays) {
  addLayersControl(m, baseGroups = c("Grey canvas", "OpenStreetMap", "Satellite"),
                   overlayGroups = overlays, options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = TRUE))
}
# Context layer shared by the interactive maps: the May 2022 network in grey
add_network <- function(m, new_links = FALSE) {
  m <- addPolylines(m, data = st_transform(net_base_sf, 4326), color = "grey", weight = 1.5,
                    opacity = 0.7, group = "Rail network")
  if (new_links) m <- addPolylines(m, data = st_transform(net_new_sf, 4326), color = "#d95f02",
                                   weight = 3, opacity = 0.8, group = "Rail network")
  m
}
# Graduated-bubble legend: circles drawn at the same radius as on the map
radius_of <- function(v, max_v, max_r = 18) 3 + (max_r - 3) * sqrt(pmax(v, 0) / max_v)
add_size_legend <- function(m, breaks, max_v, title, max_r = 18, position = "bottomleft") {
  r <- radius_of(breaks, max_v, max_r)
  cx <- cumsum(c(0, head(2 * r, -1) + 18)) + r + 6       # circles side by side
  base <- 2 * max(r) + 4
  svg <- str_c(sprintf(paste0('<circle cx="%.1f" cy="%.1f" r="%.1f" fill="#bbb" fill-opacity="0.5" ',
                              'stroke="#444"/><text x="%.1f" y="%.1f" font-size="11" ',
                              'text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">%s</text>'),
                       cx, base - r, r, cx, base + 14, comma(breaks)), collapse = "")
  addControl(m, position = position, html = str_c(
    '<div style="background:white;padding:6px 8px;border-radius:4px;font:12px sans-serif">',
    '<b>', title, '</b><br><svg width="', round(max(cx + r) + 12), '" height="', round(base + 18), '">',
    svg, '</svg></div>'))
}

# Display rule for subzone maps: hide subzones that are essentially unpopulated
# (< 100 residents or < 100 residents per km2, e.g. Murai military training area,
# 640 residents over 69 km2), so that large empty polygons do not dominate the map.
populated_for_map <- function(x) {
  x %>% filter(pop >= 100, pop / (as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 1e6) >= 100)
}
pct <- function(x, d = 1) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 10^-d)
```

# Data

## Data sources

| Data set | Source | Format | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Train Stations, May 2022 | LTA DataMall (public mirror) | CSV | Observed tap-ins and station-to-station flows |
| Train station coordinates | LTA (public mirror) | CSV | Existing station locations and codes |
| Master Plan 2025 Rail Station layer | URA via data.gov.sg | GeoJSON | Locations of future stations |
| Planned JRL/CRL1 station list | Compiled from LTA announcements | CSV | Official station codes, branches and interchanges |
| Resident population by subzone, Census 2020 | SingStat via data.gov.sg | CSV | Origin market potential |
| Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (no sea) | URA via data.gov.sg | GeoJSON | Spatial origins |
| HDB Existing Building | HDB via data.gov.sg | GeoJSON | Residential intensity (population-weighted centroids, station catchments) |
| Master Plan 2019 Land Use layer | URA, via the `home2park` R package's GitHub mirror | GeoJSON (cleaned) | Job, education and residential floor area around each station |
| Bus Stop Location (Sep 2026) | LTA DataMall, static geospatial dataset | ESRI shapefile | Feeder-bus intensity around each station |
| Train Station Exit Point (Jul 2026) | LTA DataMall, static geospatial dataset | ESRI shapefile | Independent check of station coordinates |
| OpenStreetMap points of interest (extract of 2026-11-08) | Geofabrik `malaysia-singapore-brunei-latest-free.shp.zip`, clipped to Singapore | GeoPackage (clipped) | Retail, food, education, health and leisure destinations around each station |
| Annual public transport ridership 1995–2024 | LTA via data.gov.sg | CSV | System-level context |

LTA DataMall only serves the three most recent months of OD data, so May 2022 is the most recent month for which a complete public archive was available. It is a post-COVID month with the TEL stage 3 and 4 stations not yet open, which defines the baseline network for this study.

The bus-stop and station-exit shapefiles are used exactly as downloaded from LTA DataMall. The land-use layer comes from a public GitHub mirror of URA's Master Plan 2019 release; only the land-use type and gross plot ratio (GPR) of business, commercial, white, hotel, health, educational and residential parcels are kept. The OpenStreetMap extract covers Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei; its point and polygon POI layers are clipped to Singapore's subzone boundary (@sec-quality) and saved as a single GeoPackage.

The planned-station list (`planned_stations_jrl_crl.csv`) records the 24 JRL and 12 CRL1 station codes, their branch and sequence along the line, the matching name in the URA layer, and the existing station each interchange connects to. It was compiled from LTA's published station lists because the URA layer carries names but no line, code or opening date.

## Import

```{r}
#| label: import
od_raw          <- read_csv("data/aspatial/mrt_od_202205.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
station_points  <- read_csv("data/aspatial/mrt_station_points.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
planned         <- read_csv("data/aspatial/planned_stations_jrl_crl.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pop_raw         <- read_csv("data/aspatial/resident_population_subzone_2020.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ridership_trend <- read_csv("data/aspatial/public_transport_ridership_1995_2024.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

rail_2025 <- st_read("data/geospatial/rail_station_layer_2025.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
subzones  <- st_read("data/geospatial/MP19_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
hdb       <- st_read("data/geospatial/HDBExistingBuilding.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
landuse   <- st_read("data/geospatial/mp19_landuse_attractors.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
bus_stops <- st_read("data/geospatial/BusStop.shp", quiet = TRUE)
stn_exits <- st_read("data/geospatial/Train_Station_Exit_Layer.shp", quiet = TRUE)
osm_poi   <- st_read("data/geospatial/osm_pois_sg.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

tibble(layer = c("rail_2025", "subzones", "hdb", "landuse", "bus_stops", "stn_exits", "osm_poi"),
       features = c(nrow(rail_2025), nrow(subzones), nrow(hdb), nrow(landuse), nrow(bus_stops),
                    nrow(stn_exits), nrow(osm_poi)),
       crs = c(st_crs(rail_2025)$input, st_crs(subzones)$input, st_crs(hdb)$input,
               st_crs(landuse)$input, st_crs(bus_stops)$input, st_crs(stn_exits)$input,
               st_crs(osm_poi)$input),
       epsg = c(st_crs(rail_2025)$epsg, st_crs(subzones)$epsg, st_crs(hdb)$epsg,
                st_crs(landuse)$epsg, st_crs(bus_stops)$epsg, st_crs(stn_exits)$epsg,
                st_crs(osm_poi)$epsg))
```

**Mine 0:** the layers arrive in three different reference systems. The URA and HDB layers are in WGS84 (geographic degrees); the land-use and OSM files were already projected to EPSG:3414 when they were prepared. The two LTA shapefiles declare a custom "SVY21" projection with no EPSG code, so `st_crs()$epsg` is `NA`. Its parameters (false easting 28,001.642 m, false northing 38,744.572 m, origin at 1.3667°N, 103.8333°E) are those of SVY21 / Singapore TM. The correct fix is therefore to *assign* EPSG:3414 with `st_set_crs()`; reprojecting with `st_transform()` would move every stop by the difference between two definitions of the same grid.  Distances and buffers must be computed in metres, so every layer is projected to **SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414)** before any measurement. `st_make_valid()` repairs the six self-intersecting subzone polygons found by `st_is_valid()` and the few slivers in the simplified land-use layer, so that spatial joins and intersections do not fail or silently drop features.

```{r}
#| label: project
subzones <- subzones %>% st_transform(3414) %>% st_make_valid()
hdb      <- hdb %>% st_transform(3414)
rail_2025 <- rail_2025 %>% st_transform(3414) %>% st_make_valid()
landuse  <- landuse %>% st_transform(3414) %>% st_make_valid()
# LTA shapefiles carry a custom "SVY21" definition with no EPSG code. Its parameters are
# those of SVY21 / Singapore TM, so the code is *assigned* (st_set_crs), not reprojected.
bus_stops <- bus_stops %>% st_set_crs(3414)
stn_exits <- stn_exits %>% st_set_crs(3414)
osm_poi   <- osm_poi %>% st_transform(3414)
```

The annual series (@fig-trend) puts the study month in context. May 2022 sits in the recovery phase after the 2020 collapse, so absolute volumes are below the 2019 peak. Because the Huff model allocates a fixed demand total across stations, this mostly affects the scale of predictions, not the relative ranking of stations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trend
#| fig-cap: "Average daily rail ridership, 1995–2024. The dashed line marks the OD study month (May 2022)."
#| fig-height: 4
ridership_trend %>%
  filter(mode %in% c("MRT", "LRT")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, ridership, colour = mode)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2022, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(MRT = "#176b87", LRT = "#d95f02")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average daily ridership", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Data preparation and quality assessment {#sec-quality}

The handout warns that "all data are like vast grassland full of land mines". This section documents each mine found and how it was cleared.

## Origin–destination records

```{r}
#| label: od-quality
od_raw %>%
  summarise(rows = n(),
            months = n_distinct(YEAR_MONTH),
            pt_types = n_distinct(PT_TYPE),
            hours = str_c(min(TIME_PER_HOUR), "–", max(TIME_PER_HOUR)),
            station_codes = n_distinct(c(ORIGIN_PT_CODE, DESTINATION_PT_CODE)),
            missing_values = sum(is.na(TOTAL_TRIPS)),
            negative_trips = sum(TOTAL_TRIPS < 0),
            total_trips = sum(TOTAL_TRIPS))
```

The OD file is internally clean: one month, train trips only, no missing or negative counts. Each record is a tap-in/tap-out pair aggregated by hour and day type. **Mine 1:** these are *tap-in to tap-out* journeys, so transfers inside the paid area are invisible. A trip from an LRT station to the CBD is recorded once, at its LRT origin. Tap-ins are therefore a clean measure of where people *enter* the network, which is exactly what a residential catchment model predicts.

## Existing stations

```{r}
#| label: station-xy-check
xy_missing <- station_points %>% filter(is.na(X) | is.na(Y))

xy_check <- station_points %>%
  filter(!is.na(X)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(3414) %>%
  mutate(dev_m = sqrt((st_coordinates(.)[, 1] - X)^2 + (st_coordinates(.)[, 2] - Y)^2))

xy_missing %>% select(STN_NAME, STN_NO, X, Y, Latitude, Longitude)
summary(xy_check$dev_m)

# Which coordinate is right where the two disagree? Test both against the URA station footprints.
ura_footprint <- rail_2025 %>% mutate(name = str_squish(NAME))
fp_dist <- function(pt, nm) min(as.numeric(st_distance(pt, ura_footprint[ura_footprint$name == nm, ])))

xy_disagree <- xy_check %>%
  filter(dev_m > 50) %>%
  mutate(name = str_remove(STN_NAME, " (MRT|LRT) STATION$"))

xy_disagree %>%
  mutate(latlon_to_footprint_m = map_dbl(seq_len(n()), \(i) fp_dist(st_geometry(xy_disagree)[i], name[i])),
         xy_to_footprint_m = map_dbl(seq_len(n()), \(i)
           fp_dist(st_sfc(st_point(c(X[i], Y[i])), crs = 3414), name[i]))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(STN_NAME, STN_NO, dev_m = round(dev_m),
            latlon_to_footprint_m = round(latlon_to_footprint_m),
            xy_to_footprint_m = round(xy_to_footprint_m))
```

**Mine 2:** the station file stores each location twice, as SVY21 `X`/`Y` and as WGS84 latitude/longitude, and the two disagree.

- The five TEL stage 2 stations have **no `X`/`Y`** at all. Building the layer from `X`/`Y` alone would drop them or fail.
- For the other 162 stations, projected latitude/longitude lies within a median of `r fmt(median(xy_check$dev_m), 1)` m of `X`/`Y`, but three stations disagree by more than 100 m. Testing both points against the URA station footprints settles which is right. For **Rochor**, the latitude/longitude is about 350 m away from the station while `X`/`Y` falls inside its footprint. For Little India and Outram Park, both points fall inside the large multi-line footprints.

The rule adopted is therefore: **use the native SVY21 `X`/`Y` where present, and projected latitude/longitude only for the five stations without it**. The original version of this analysis used latitude/longitude throughout and so misplaced Rochor.

```{r}
#| label: station-operational
od_codes <- unique(c(od_raw$ORIGIN_PT_CODE, od_raw$DESTINATION_PT_CODE))

non_operational <- tribble(
  ~stn_code, ~station, ~status_may_2022,
  "BP14", "Ten Mile Junction", "Bukit Panjang LRT station closed in January 2019",
  "CC18", "Bukit Brown",       "Shell station built in 2009 but never opened",
  "PW2",  "Teck Lee",          "Punggol LRT station opened only in August 2024")

stopifnot(all(non_operational$stn_code %in% setdiff(station_points$STN_NO, od_codes)))
non_operational
```

**Mine 3:** three codes in the station file never appear in the OD data. They are not join errors. They are stations that carried no passengers in May 2022, and one of them, **Bukit Brown, is itself a ghost station**. Keeping them would add three "observed zero" stations to the calibration and bias the model downwards, so they are removed. All remaining 164 station codes match the OD codes exactly, including the combined interchange codes such as `NS24/NE6/CC1`.

```{r}
#| label: stations-existing
latlon_svy21 <- station_points %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(3414) %>% st_coordinates()

stations <- station_points %>%
  mutate(x = coalesce(X, latlon_svy21[, 1]), y = coalesce(Y, latlon_svy21[, 2])) %>%
  filter(!STN_NO %in% non_operational$stn_code) %>%
  transmute(stn_code = STN_NO,
            stn_name = str_squish(str_remove(STN_NAME, " (MRT|LRT) STATION$")),
            x, y) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 3414)

nrow(stations)
```

The LTA station-exit layer gives an independent check of the adopted coordinates: every station point should lie within a short walk of its own exits.

```{r}
#| label: station-exit-check
exits_named <- stn_exits %>%
  mutate(stn_name = str_squish(str_remove(stn_name, " (MRT|LRT) STATION$")))

exit_check <- stations %>%
  mutate(nearest_own_exit_m = map_dbl(seq_len(n()), \(i) {
    own <- exits_named[exits_named$stn_name == stn_name[i], ]
    if (nrow(own) == 0) NA_real_ else min(as.numeric(st_distance(st_geometry(stations)[i], own)))
  })) %>% st_drop_geometry()

rochor_latlon <- station_points %>% filter(STN_NO == "DT13") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) %>% st_transform(3414)

tibble(stations_matched_to_exits = sum(!is.na(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m)),
       median_m = median(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m, na.rm = TRUE),
       p95_m = quantile(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
       rochor_adopted_m = exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m[exit_check$stn_code == "DT13"],
       rochor_latlon_m = min(as.numeric(st_distance(rochor_latlon,
                                                    exits_named[exits_named$stn_name == "ROCHOR", ]))))
```

`r sum(!is.na(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m))` of the 164 stations match their exits by name, and the adopted point lies a median of `r fmt(median(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m, na.rm = TRUE))` m from its nearest exit. Rochor's adopted `X`/`Y` point is `r fmt(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m[exit_check$stn_code == "DT13"])` m from an exit, while its latitude/longitude point would have been `r fmt(min(as.numeric(st_distance(rochor_latlon, exits_named[exits_named$stn_name == "ROCHOR", ]))))` m away. This confirms the coordinate rule above with a second, independent LTA source.

## Future stations: auditing the URA rail layer

The URA Master Plan 2025 layer contains polygons for every existing *and* planned station footprint, identified only by name. A naive approach (keep every URA name that does not match an existing station name) treats all of them as "future" stations.

```{r}
#| label: ura-audit
ura_names <- rail_2025 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(raw = NAME, ura_name = str_squish(NAME)) %>%
  distinct()

naive_new <- setdiff(ura_names$raw, stations$stn_name)

opened_after_may22 <- c("ORCHARD BOULEVARD", "GREAT WORLD", "HAVELOCK", "MAXWELL",
                        "SHENTON WAY", "GARDEN BY THE BAY", "NAPIER", "TANJONG RHU",
                        "KATONG PARK", "TANJONG KATONG", "MARINE PARADE",
                        "MARINE TERRACE", "SIGLAP", "BAYSHORE", "HUME", "PUNGGOL COAST",
                        "TECK LEE")
sentosa_express <- c("BEACH", "IMBIAH", "RESORTS WORLD")
spelling_alias  <- c("ONE NORTH" = "ONE-NORTH", "JELEPANG" = "JELAPANG")

ura_audit <- ura_names %>%
  filter(raw %in% naive_new) %>%
  mutate(category = case_when(
    ura_name %in% planned$ura_name ~ "1. JRL / CRL1 station (in scope)",
    ura_name %in% stations$stn_name |
      str_remove(ura_name, " INTERCHANGE$") %in% stations$stn_name |
      ura_name %in% names(spelling_alias) ~
      "2. Existing station under a variant name",
    ura_name %in% opened_after_may22 ~ "3. Opened after May 2022 (TEL 3–4, Hume, Punggol Coast, Teck Lee)",
    ura_name %in% sentosa_express ~ "4. Sentosa Express (not in LTA OD data)",
    TRUE ~ "5. Other future line, unopened shell or annotation code"))

ura_audit %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), examples = str_c(head(ura_name, 6), collapse = ", "))
```

**Mine 4:** the naive approach flags `r length(naive_new)` "future" stations, but only `r sum(ura_audit$category == "1. JRL / CRL1 station (in scope)")` of them belong to the JRL or CRL1. The rest are:

- existing stations spelt differently (trailing spaces, or the suffix "INTERCHANGE" on, for example, *Bishan Interchange*);
- stations that opened after the study month;
- the Sentosa monorail;
- stations on lines beyond 2030, plus annotation codes such as `DE1` and `NS6`.

Treating these as new stations would have placed duplicate "competitors" on top of existing stations such as Bishan and Serangoon and split their demand artificially.

The in-scope stations are taken from the official station list. Of the 36 JRL/CRL1 stations, **7 are interchanges with existing stations**: Choa Chu Kang, Boon Lay, Jurong East, Pasir Ris, Hougang, Ang Mo Kio and Bright Hill. These are not new locations; the existing station gains a line. The remaining **29 are genuinely new**, and their coordinates come from the URA station footprints.

```{r}
#| label: planned-stations
ura_points <- rail_2025 %>%
  mutate(ura_name = str_squish(NAME)) %>%
  group_by(ura_name) %>%
  summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry), .groups = "drop") %>%
  st_point_on_surface()

planned <- planned %>% mutate(ura_name = str_squish(ura_name))

new_stations <- planned %>%
  filter(is.na(interchange_with)) %>%
  left_join(ura_points, by = "ura_name") %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  transmute(stn_code, stn_name, line)

interchange_upgrades <- planned %>% filter(!is.na(interchange_with))

stopifnot(nrow(new_stations) == 29, !any(st_is_empty(new_stations)),
          all(interchange_upgrades$interchange_with %in% stations$stn_code))

new_stations %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(line, name = "new_stations")
```

The scenario therefore compares two networks:

- **Base**: the May 2022 network of 164 stations.
- **Expanded**: the base plus 29 new JRL/CRL1 stations, with 7 existing stations upgraded to interchanges.

Stations that opened between June 2022 and 2026 (TEL 3–4, Hume, Punggol Coast, Teck Lee) are deliberately left out of both networks, so that the difference between the two networks isolates the effect of the JRL and CRL1.

## Station attributes and the rail network graph

Each station code is split into its line prefix (`NS`, `EW`, `CG`, …), and prefixes are grouped into line families (for example, `CG` belongs to the East-West Line and `CE` to the Circle Line). Two attraction variables follow:

- `n_lines`: the number of distinct line families serving the station. Interchanges score 2 or 3.
- `lrt`: TRUE for stations served only by LRT. LRT stations act as feeders inside towns and offer a lower level of service than MRT stations.

A network graph is also built by linking consecutive station numbers along each line, plus the branch and loop connections (the Changi Airport branch, the Circle Line extension and the LRT loops). Edges are weighted by straight-line length. The graph provides network distances for the SIM and a closeness-centrality candidate for the Huff attraction.

```{r}
#| label: network-functions
line_family <- function(prefix) {
  case_when(prefix %in% c("EW", "CG") ~ "EWL", prefix %in% c("CC", "CE") ~ "CCL",
            prefix == "NS" ~ "NSL", prefix == "NE" ~ "NEL", prefix == "DT" ~ "DTL",
            prefix == "TE" ~ "TEL", prefix == "BP" ~ "BPLRT",
            prefix %in% c("SE", "SW", "STC") ~ "SKLRT",
            prefix %in% c("PE", "PW", "PTC") ~ "PGLRT",
            prefix %in% c("JS", "JW", "JE") ~ "JRL", prefix == "CR" ~ "CRL")
}

explode_codes <- function(stn_tbl) {
  stn_tbl %>%
    select(stn_code) %>%
    mutate(code = str_split(stn_code, "/")) %>%
    unnest(code) %>%
    mutate(prefix = str_extract(code, "^[A-Z]+"),
           num    = as.integer(str_extract(code, "[0-9]+$")),
           family = line_family(prefix))
}

build_edges <- function(codes, xy) {
  hub <- function(code) codes$stn_code[codes$code == code]
  ends <- function(p) { x <- codes %>% filter(prefix == p) %>% arrange(num)
                        c(first(x$stn_code), last(x$stn_code)) }
  seq_edges <- codes %>% filter(!is.na(num)) %>% arrange(prefix, num) %>%
    group_by(prefix) %>% mutate(to = lead(stn_code)) %>% ungroup() %>%
    filter(!is.na(to)) %>% transmute(from = stn_code, to)
  links <- bind_rows(
    tibble(from = hub("EW4"),  to = hub("CG1")),       # Changi Airport branch
    tibble(from = hub("CC4"),  to = hub("CE1")),       # Circle Line extension
    tibble(from = hub("BP13"), to = hub("BP6")),       # Bukit Panjang LRT loop
    tibble(from = hub("STC"),  to = c(ends("SE"), ends("SW"))),   # Sengkang LRT loops
    tibble(from = hub("PTC"),  to = c(ends("PE"), ends("PW"))))   # Punggol LRT loops
  if (any(codes$prefix == "JE")) links <- bind_rows(links,
    tibble(from = hub("JS3"), to = hub("JE1")),        # JRL East branch at Tengah
    tibble(from = hub("JS7"), to = hub("JW1")))        # JRL West branch at Bahar Junction
  bind_rows(seq_edges, links) %>% distinct() %>%
    mutate(w_km = sqrt(rowSums((xy[from, ] - xy[to, ])^2)) / 1000)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: network-base
codes_base <- explode_codes(st_drop_geometry(stations))
xy_base <- st_coordinates(stations); rownames(xy_base) <- stations$stn_code
edges_base <- build_edges(codes_base, xy_base)
g_base <- graph_from_data_frame(edges_base, directed = FALSE, vertices = stations$stn_code)

station_attr <- codes_base %>%
  group_by(stn_code) %>%
  summarise(n_lines = n_distinct(family), lrt = all(str_detect(family, "LRT")), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(closeness = closeness(g_base, weights = edges_base$w_km, normalized = TRUE)[stn_code])

c(connected = is_connected(g_base), nodes = vcount(g_base), edges = ecount(g_base))
station_attr %>% count(n_lines, lrt)
```

The graph is connected (164 nodes). There are 137 single-line stations, 26 two-line interchanges and one three-line interchange (Dhoby Ghaut), and 37 stations are LRT-only.

The expanded network reuses the same functions. Each JRL/CRL1 code is attached to its interchange station, or added as a new node, and the two JRL branches are linked at Tengah and Bahar Junction.

```{r}
#| label: network-expanded
stations_exp <- bind_rows(
  stations %>% mutate(status = "Existing"),
  new_stations %>% transmute(stn_code, stn_name, status = "New (JRL/CRL1)"))

codes_exp <- bind_rows(
  codes_base,
  planned %>% transmute(code = stn_code, stn_code = coalesce(interchange_with, stn_code)) %>%
    mutate(prefix = str_extract(code, "^[A-Z]+"), num = as.integer(str_extract(code, "[0-9]+$")),
           family = line_family(prefix)))

xy_exp <- st_coordinates(stations_exp); rownames(xy_exp) <- stations_exp$stn_code
edges_exp <- build_edges(codes_exp, xy_exp)
g_exp <- graph_from_data_frame(edges_exp, directed = FALSE, vertices = stations_exp$stn_code)

station_attr_exp <- codes_exp %>%
  group_by(stn_code) %>%
  summarise(n_lines = n_distinct(family), lrt = all(str_detect(family, "LRT")), .groups = "drop")

stations_exp <- stations_exp %>% left_join(station_attr_exp, by = "stn_code")
c(connected = is_connected(g_exp), nodes = vcount(g_exp),
  upgraded_interchanges = sum(station_attr_exp$n_lines[match(interchange_upgrades$interchange_with,
                                                       station_attr_exp$stn_code)] >
                              station_attr$n_lines[match(interchange_upgrades$interchange_with,
                                                         station_attr$stn_code)]))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-network
#| fig-cap: "The rail network graph used in the analysis. Grey lines and dots show the May 2022 network; orange shows the JRL and CRL Phase 1 links and the 29 new stations."
#| fig-height: 6.5
edge_lines <- function(edges, xy) {
  st_sfc(pmap(list(edges$from, edges$to),
              \(a, b) st_linestring(rbind(xy[a, ], xy[b, ]))), crs = 3414) %>%
    st_sf(geometry = .)
}
net_base_sf <- edge_lines(edges_base, xy_exp)
net_new_sf  <- edge_lines(anti_join(edges_exp, edges_base, by = c("from", "to")), xy_exp)

tm_shape(subzones) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey97", col = "grey85", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(net_base_sf) + tm_lines(col = "grey45", lwd = 1.2) +
  tm_shape(net_new_sf) + tm_lines(col = "#d95f02", lwd = 2.2) +
  tm_shape(stations) + tm_dots(fill = "grey30", size = 0.12) +
  tm_shape(new_stations) + tm_dots(fill = "#d95f02", size = 0.25) +
  tm_shape(new_stations %>% filter(stn_code %in% c("JS3", "JW3", "JE7", "CR2", "CR10"))) +
  tm_text("stn_name", size = 0.55, ymod = 0.7, col = "#a63f00") +
  tm_title("Base network (May 2022) and JRL / CRL1 extensions") +
  tm_compass(position = c("right", "top"), size = 1.5) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
```

The JRL fills the large rail gap in the Jurong–Tengah–NTU area, which the existing EWL serves only along its southern edge. CRL1 adds an orbital link through Pasir Ris, Tampines North, Hougang and Ang Mo Kio. It crosses all four radial lines and so offers a north-eastern bypass of the congested city centre. The map makes the first planning question obvious: the JRL serves some of the emptiest land in the dataset (Tengah, the Jurong industrial belt), whereas CRL1 cuts through mature, dense towns.

## Origins: resident market potential

```{r}
#| label: population-clean
pop <- pop_raw %>%
  filter(Number != "Total", !str_detect(str_to_upper(Number), "- ?TOTAL$")) %>%
  transmute(SUBZONE_N = str_to_upper(str_squish(Number)),
            pop = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Total_Total)))

tibble(subzone_rows = nrow(pop),
       dash_values_coded_zero = sum(is.na(pop$pop)),
       unmatched_in_boundary = length(setdiff(pop$SUBZONE_N, str_to_upper(subzones$SUBZONE_N))),
       total_residents = sum(pop$pop, na.rm = TRUE))
```

**Mine 5:** the Census table mixes planning-area subtotal rows ("Ang Mo Kio - Total") with subzone rows, and one subtotal uses a different spelling ("CHANGI- TOTAL"). It also codes nil population as "-". Both kinds of subtotal are removed with a pattern that tolerates the missing space. A "-" is converted to 0, not to NA, because SingStat uses it for "nil". After cleaning, every Census subzone matches a boundary polygon, and the total of 4,044,210 residents (rounding aside) matches the published national figure.

A centroid is a poor proxy for where people actually live in large subzones that are mostly industrial land, parkland or reservoir. **Population-weighted centroids** are therefore computed as the footprint-area-weighted mean location of HDB blocks within each subzone. Subzones without HDB blocks (landed or condominium estates) fall back to `st_point_on_surface()`.

```{r}
#| label: origins
hdb_pt <- hdb %>%
  mutate(area_m2 = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_point_on_surface() %>%
  select(area_m2)

hdb_centroids <- hdb_pt %>%
  st_join(subzones %>% select(SUBZONE_N)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(SUBZONE_N)) %>%
  mutate(x = st_coordinates(.)[, 1], y = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(SUBZONE_N) %>%
  summarise(cx = weighted.mean(x, area_m2), cy = weighted.mean(y, area_m2),
            hdb_blocks = n(), .groups = "drop")

make_origins <- function(sz) {
  pos <- st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(sz)))
  sz %>%
    left_join(hdb_centroids, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
    mutate(ox = coalesce(cx, pos[, 1]), oy = coalesce(cy, pos[, 2]),
           centroid = if_else(is.na(cx), "Point on surface", "HDB-weighted"))
}

origins_poly <- subzones %>%
  left_join(pop, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  mutate(pop = replace_na(pop, 0)) %>%
  filter(pop > 0) %>%
  make_origins() %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, REGION_N, pop, ox, oy, centroid)

origins_pt <- origins_poly %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("ox", "oy"), crs = 3414)

origins_poly %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(centroid) %>% summarise(subzones = n(), residents = sum(pop))
```

## Observed station demand and destination attributes

The dependent variable is **weekday morning-peak (06:00–09:59) tap-ins** at each station, summed over May 2022. This choice follows Chapter 15's morning-peak convention and fits the Huff logic. Morning-peak boardings are overwhelmingly home-based, so they are the trips generated by resident population. Total daily ridership (tap-ins plus tap-outs) also counts trips *attracted* by jobs and malls, which no residential model can explain. Total ridership is kept as a secondary measure for context.

Several station attributes are also derived for each of the 193 stations, using catchments of roughly a 10-minute walk (800 m) or a 5-minute walk (400 m):

- **HDB footprint within 800 m**: residential intensity;
- **job, education and residential floor area within 800 m**, from the Master Plan land use (parcel area × gross plot ratio). Because the Master Plan records *planned* land use, it already contains the Jurong Innovation District and the Tengah town, which is exactly what is needed to describe stations that do not exist yet;
- **bus stops within 400 m**: the number of LTA bus stops within 400 m, a measure of feeder-bus access;
- **OSM points of interest within 800 m**, grouped into food & retail, education, health, and leisure & civic destinations (@sec-va-mci).

```{r}
#| label: destinations
am_peak <- od_raw %>% filter(DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY", between(TIME_PER_HOUR, 6, 9))

demand <- stations %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(stn_code) %>%
  left_join(am_peak %>% count(stn_code = ORIGIN_PT_CODE, wt = TOTAL_TRIPS, name = "am_tapin"),
            by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(od_raw %>% count(stn_code = ORIGIN_PT_CODE, wt = TOTAL_TRIPS, name = "all_tapin"),
            by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(od_raw %>% count(stn_code = DESTINATION_PT_CODE, wt = TOTAL_TRIPS, name = "all_tapout"),
            by = "stn_code") %>%
  mutate(total_ridership = all_tapin + all_tapout)

hdb800 <- st_join(st_buffer(stations_exp %>% select(stn_code), 800), hdb_pt) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(stn_code) %>%
  summarise(hdb_ha_800m = sum(area_m2, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e4, .groups = "drop")

weekdays_may22 <- 19   # 22 Mon–Fri minus Labour Day (2 May), Hari Raya Puasa (3 May), Vesak (16 May)

# Land-use attractors within 800 m: floor area = parcel area x gross plot ratio (GPR).
# GPR is "EVA" (subject to evaluation) or missing for some parcels; these count at GPR = 1.
lu_typed <- landuse %>%
  mutate(gpr_num = coalesce(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(GPR)), 1),
         type = case_when(str_detect(LU_DESC, "BUSINESS|COMMERCIAL|WHITE|HOTEL|HEALTH") ~ "job_ha",
                          LU_DESC == "EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTION" ~ "edu_ha",
                          TRUE ~ "res_ha"))

lu_800 <- st_intersection(st_buffer(stations_exp %>% select(stn_code), 800),
                          lu_typed %>% select(type, gpr_num)) %>%
  mutate(floor_ha = as.numeric(st_area(.)) * if_else(type == "edu_ha", 1, gpr_num) / 1e4) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(stn_code, type) %>% summarise(floor_ha = sum(floor_ha), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = floor_ha, values_fill = 0)

bus_400 <- st_join(st_buffer(stations_exp %>% select(stn_code), 400),
                   bus_stops %>% select(BUS_STOP_N)) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(stn_code) %>% summarise(bus_stops_400m = sum(!is.na(BUS_STOP_N)), .groups = "drop")

# OSM points of interest within 800 m, grouped with Geofabrik's thematic code ranges
# (23xx catering, 25xx shops, 26xx money; 21xx health; 20xx/22xx/27xx public, leisure, tourism).
# Street furniture (benches, bins, vending machines, 29xx) is excluded.
poi_grouped <- osm_poi %>%
  mutate(group = case_when(
    code %/% 100 %in% c(23, 25, 26) ~ "poi_food_retail",
    fclass %in% c("school", "university", "college", "kindergarten") ~ "poi_edu",
    code %/% 100 == 21 ~ "poi_health",
    code %/% 100 %in% c(20, 22, 27) ~ "poi_leisure_civic")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(group))

poi_800 <- st_join(st_buffer(stations_exp %>% select(stn_code), 800), poi_grouped %>% select(group)) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>% filter(!is.na(group)) %>%
  count(stn_code, group) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

attractors <- stations_exp %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(stn_code) %>%
  left_join(lu_800, by = "stn_code") %>% left_join(bus_400, by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(poi_800, by = "stn_code") %>%
  mutate(across(-stn_code, \(x) replace_na(x, 0)))

summary(demand %>% select(am_tapin, total_ridership))
count(st_drop_geometry(poi_grouped), group)
summary(attractors %>% select(-stn_code))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-observed

pop_density <- subzones %>%
  left_join(pop, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%

obs_map <- stations %>% left_join(demand, by = "stn_code") %>% mutate(am_day = am_tapin / weekdays_may22)

tm_shape(pop_density) +

              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residents per km²"),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.2) +
  tm_shape(obs_map) +
```
